set.statement: In people taking part in 572 case–control and cohort studies published from 1956 to 2012 (486,538 people with cancer; 41% of the studies from North America, 32% from Europe and 18% from Asia), drinking more than 12.5 g of ethanol a day on average (more than one drink as the review defines it) compared with not drinking (nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 24% of the studies; former drinkers were not separated) is associated with more cancers of the mouth and pharynx, the oesophagus (squamous cell carcinoma only), the larynx, the colon and rectum and the female breast, and, at heavy drinking, of the liver, with the relative risk rising with the amount (Bagnardi et al., 2015; funded by Italian cancer-research charities, no conflicts declared). The review reports no absolute risks, so its ratios cannot be turned into numbers out of 100. For heavy drinking (above 50 g a day, more than four drinks) the pooled relative risks were 5.13 (95% CI 4.31–6.10) for the mouth and pharynx, 4.95 (3.86–6.34) for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, 2.65 (2.19–3.19) for the larynx, 2.07 (1.66–2.58) for the liver, 1.61 (1.33–1.94) for the breast (from 11 of the 118 breast studies, editors' count) and 1.44 (1.25–1.65) for the colon and rectum; for moderate drinking (above 12.5 and up to 50 g a day) they were 1.83 (1.62–2.07), 2.23 (1.87–2.65), 1.44 (1.25–1.66), 1.08 (0.97–1.20, no clear difference), 1.23 (1.19–1.28) and 1.17 (1.11–1.24). The colorectal association differed by sex (P = 0.010): it was clear in men (heavy drinking 1.53, 1.30–1.80) but not in women (moderate 1.07, 0.99–1.16; heavy 1.24, 0.68–2.25, from 4 studies). Heavy drinking was also associated with cancers of the stomach (1.21, 1.07–1.36), pancreas (1.19, 1.11–1.28), lung (1.15, 1.02–1.30) and gallbladder (2.64, 1.62–4.30; 8 studies of this cancer in all), and the authors say that smoking not fully taken into account may explain part of the lung and stomach results (their earlier review found no link with lung cancer in people who never smoked); moderate drinking went with small increases in prostate cancer (1.06, 1.01–1.11) and melanoma (1.20, 1.03–1.41), clear only in North American studies (and, for melanoma, in the two cohort studies), although the differences between regions were not statistically significant; there was no clear association with adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus and gastric cardia or with cancers of the small intestine, cervix, endometrium, ovary, bladder or brain; and cancers of the kidney and thyroid and both kinds of lymphoma were less common in people who drank (for example non-Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.75, 0.64–0.88, at heavy drinking): for the lymphomas the authors suggest that people stop or cut down when early symptoms start, while they read the kidney result both as protection and, in their conclusion, as no association (the World Cancer Research Fund rates a lower kidney cancer risk at up to 30 g a day as probable, as relayed by Rumgay et al., 2021). The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study, whose review of studies probably overlaps with this one (its study list was not read), fitted risk curves that rise with intake for every cancer it included (Griswold et al., 2018). Results varied widely between studies (I² up to 91%); only 297 of the 572 studies reported adjusted estimates, so differences in smoking and other habits were often not taken into account, although the authors report that keeping only adjusted estimates did not materially change the results (figures in a supplement not read); case–control studies gave stronger associations than cohort studies at some sites (heavy drinking and liver cancer 2.79 against 1.12; larynx 2.81 against 1.12), a difference statistically clear for the mouth and pharynx (P = 0.007) but not for the liver or larynx (P = 0.226 and 0.216); and the review neither appraised the studies nor tested for publication bias. That alcohol causes cancer at these sites is the judgment of the International Agency for Research on Cancer, whose list a 2021 cancer-burden model used (Rumgay et al., 2021); this pooling of observational studies cannot show it by itself. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: Across 572 studies, people who drank more than about one drink a day (12.5 g of alcohol) had more cancer of the mouth and throat, of one type of gullet cancer, of the voice box, of the bowel and of the breast than people who did not drink, and people who drank more than four drinks a day also had more liver cancer. At more than four drinks a day, mouth and throat cancer and that gullet cancer were about 5 times as common, voice-box cancer about 2.7 times, liver cancer about 2 times, breast cancer about 1.6 times and bowel cancer about 1.4 times. The bowel cancer link was clear in men but not in women. The review gives no numbers out of 100. Kidney and thyroid cancer and cancers of the lymph glands were less common in people who drank; for the lymph glands, the authors think this partly reflects people cutting down when they first feel ill. Results varied a lot between studies, about half the studies did not take smoking or other differences into account (though the authors say that leaving those studies out changed little), and the review did not check the studies' quality. An international cancer agency judges that alcohol causes these cancers; this review alone cannot show it.

set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Bagnardi et al. (card sc_bagnardi_2015: AMSTAR 2 critically low): no protocol, no appraisal of the primary studies, and adjusted estimates pooled with crude ones (297 of 572 studies adjusted); case–control studies, open to recall and control-selection bias, are 409 of the 572 and gave stronger associations than cohorts at several sites; residual confounding by smoking is possible for the mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, larynx, lung and stomach. Counted once. The authors report that keeping only adjusted estimates did not materially change the results, but those figures are in a supplement that was not read.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: I² reaches 91% at heavy drinking, so the size differs widely between studies, but for the main sites the direction is the same across designs, sexes and world regions (Tables 2 to 4), and the claim gives design-specific figures rather than one number; not rated down. The colorectal association was clear in men but not in women (heterogeneity P = 0.010; women, heavy drinking 1.24, 0.68–2.25, from 4 studies), which the statement reports; the direction is positive in both sexes.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; it is rated down one level for risk of bias and up one level for the dose–response gradient, which gives low; a strict reading without the upgrade would give very low. Rated as worded: an association that grows with the amount; that alcohol causes these cancers is the classification of the International Agency for Research on Cancer, cited by the papers, and is not tested by this pooling. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 review probably shares many primary studies with this one (its study list was not read), and the 2021 model only uses IARC's list, so neither is counted as independent replication. Status replicated: independent subsets of the 572 studies, by design, sex and world region, agree in direction for the main sites.

set.statement: In people taking part in the same 572 case–control and cohort studies (Bagnardi et al., 2015), light drinking (up to 12.5 g of ethanol a day on average, one drink or less as the review defines it) compared with not drinking (nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 24% of the studies; former drinkers not separated) is associated with slightly more of some cancers and slightly fewer of others, with no absolute risks reported: pooled relative risks of 1.13 (95% CI 1.00–1.26) for cancers of the mouth and pharynx, 1.26 (1.06–1.50) for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, 1.04 (1.01–1.07) for female breast cancer and 1.04 (1.01–1.08) for prostate cancer (from 26, 34, 115 and 36 studies; editors' counts from the review's Table 2); no clear difference for cancers of the colon and rectum (0.99, 0.95–1.04), liver (1.00, 0.85–1.18) or larynx (0.87, 0.68–1.11); and lower figures for lung cancer (0.84, 0.79–0.88), adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus and gastric cardia (0.86, 0.76–0.98), cancers of the kidney (0.92, 0.86–0.99) and thyroid (0.81, 0.74–0.88), and both kinds of lymphoma (Hodgkin's 0.73, 0.59–0.89; non-Hodgkin's 0.88, 0.80–0.97). Differences this small can be produced or hidden by people who drink more reporting less, which the authors say may partly or largely explain the light-drinking associations, by smoking and other differences (only 297 of the 572 studies reported adjusted estimates), and by former or occasional drinkers among the comparison group; the authors report that keeping only adjusted estimates, or dropping studies with occasional drinkers in the comparison group, did not materially change the results (figures in a supplement not read). The raised figures also depend on how the studies are split: for the mouth and pharynx the light-drinking figure was 1.22 (1.10–1.35) in case–control studies, which ask about drinking after the cancer is found, but 0.86 (0.60–1.23) in cohort studies, while for the breast it was 1.06 (1.03–1.10) in cohort studies and 1.04 (0.99–1.09) in case–control studies; the mouth, pharynx and oesophagus figures were statistically clear in men (1.20 and 1.39) but not in women and, by world region, only in Asian studies (1.33 and 1.54), where the authors point to a common variant of a gene for breaking down alcohol, although the regions did not differ significantly (P = 0.375 and 0.503). The lower lung and oesophageal adenocarcinoma figures appear in the review's figure but not in its text, and its continuous dose–response model found a slight rise in lung cancer risk with intake and no trend for oesophageal adenocarcinoma. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study fitted risk curves that rise with intake for each of the eight cancers it modelled, which did not include kidney, thyroid or lymphoma (Griswold et al., 2018; list as given by Bryazka et al., 2022), and a model of cancers in 2020 attributes 41,300 new cases worldwide (95% uncertainty interval 35,400–145,800) to drinking up to 10 g a day, against lifetime abstention, counting only cancers that the International Agency for Research on Cancer lists as caused by alcohol, leaving out a probable protective association with kidney cancer and counting former drinkers as unexposed (Rumgay et al., 2021); both depend on the shape of the risk curves at low intake, which is what these studies leave uncertain. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
set.plain: In the same studies, people who had up to about one drink a day (12.5 g of alcohol) had slightly more mouth and throat cancer (1.13 times, a borderline result), one type of gullet cancer (1.26 times), breast cancer (1.04 times) and prostate cancer (1.04 times) than people who did not drink, and slightly less lung, kidney and thyroid cancer and cancer of the lymph glands. The review gives no numbers out of 100. The mouth and throat result came from studies that asked people about their drinking after their cancer was found, not from studies that followed people over time; the breast result was clearer in studies that followed people over time. Differences this small could come from people who drink more saying they drink less, from smoking and other differences, or from people who had stopped drinking being counted with people who did not drink. A model estimated that drinking up to 10 g a day caused about 41,000 new cancers worldwide in 2020, compared with no one ever drinking; that figure depends on the shape of the risk curves at low amounts, which is what these studies leave uncertain.
set.magnitude: Bagnardi et al. 2015, light drinking against nondrinkers or occasional drinkers (pooled RR, 95% CI; I²; studies, editors' count from Table 2): mouth and pharynx 1.13 (1.00–1.26; 26%; 26 studies); oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 1.26 (1.06–1.50; 68%; 34); female breast 1.04 (1.01–1.07; 63%; 115); prostate 1.04 (1.01–1.08; 36); colon and rectum 0.99 (0.95–1.04); liver 1.00 (0.85–1.18); larynx 0.87 (0.68–1.11); lung 0.84 (0.79–0.88); oesophageal adenocarcinoma and gastric cardia 0.86 (0.76–0.98); kidney 0.92 (0.86–0.99); thyroid 0.81 (0.74–0.88); Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.73 (0.59–0.89); non-Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.88 (0.80–0.97). By design, cohort against case–control studies: mouth and pharynx 0.86 (0.60–1.23) against 1.22 (1.10–1.35); breast 1.06 (1.03–1.10) against 1.04 (0.99–1.09). By sex: mouth and pharynx men 1.20 (1.06–1.35), women 1.00 (0.78–1.27); oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma men 1.39 (1.11–1.74), women 1.14 (0.87–1.49). Asian studies only: mouth and pharynx 1.33 (1.06–1.68; 7 studies), oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 1.54 (1.18–2.00; 11 studies); between-area heterogeneity P = 0.375 and 0.503. Rumgay et al. 2021 (model): 41,300 (35,400–145,800) new cancers in 2020 attributed to intake up to 10 g a day against lifetime abstention.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: As for the moderate and heavy estimates (card sc_bagnardi_2015: AMSTAR 2 critically low), and at light intake the biases are as large as the associations: under-reporting moves people who drink more into the light category, former and occasional drinkers in the reference group can move the estimates either way, and about half the estimates are crude; the authors concede that under-reporting may partly or largely explain the light-drinking associations. In the review's own splits, the mouth and pharynx excess comes from case–control studies, which are open to recall bias (1.22 against 0.86 in cohort studies), while the breast excess is clearer in cohort studies (1.06).
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Positive associations at some sites and inverse ones at others (lung, oesophageal adenocarcinoma, kidney, thyroid, lymphomas); within sites, the mouth and pharynx excess appears in case–control but not cohort studies (heterogeneity P = 0.007), the oral and oesophageal excesses were clear in men and in Asian studies only, although the regional differences were not significant (P = 0.375 and 0.503), and the review's continuous model shows a slight rise in lung cancer risk where its light-drinking category shows 0.84; I² 26% to 68% for the positive estimates; no adequate explanation.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is rated down one level each for risk of bias and inconsistency, which is below the floor, so very low. Rated as worded: small associations in both directions at light intake, site by site; with these data none can be told apart from bias, and the review's own splits by design, sex and region do not agree on where the excess lies. The Global Burden of Disease curves probably draw on many of the same studies and cover only eight cancers, and the 2020 model's low-intake figure rests on the shape of its curves at low intake, so neither is independent support. Status mixed: findings differ by site, by design and by region without an adequate explanation.

set.statement: In the world's population in 2020, alcohol drinking compared with a counterfactual in which no one had ever drunk (lifetime abstention) is estimated by one modelling study to account for 741,300 new cancer cases (95% uncertainty interval 558,500–951,200), about 4 in every 100 new cancers (4.1%, 3.1%–5.3%; non-melanoma skin cancer excluded): about 6 in 100 new cancers in men (568,700 cases; 6.1%) and 2 in 100 in women (172,600; 2.0%) (Rumgay et al., 2021; no funding, no competing interests declared). The model includes only the cancers that the International Agency for Research on Cancer judges to be caused by alcohol: oesophagus (squamous cell carcinoma only) 189,700 cases, 31.6% of all oesophageal cancers; liver (hepatocellular carcinoma only) 154,700, 17.3% of all liver cancers; female breast 98,300, 4.4%; colon 91,500, 8.1%; lip and oral cavity 74,900, 20.2%; rectum 65,100, 9.0%; pharynx 39,400, 22.0%; and larynx 27,600, 15.0%. It attributes 346,400 cases (46.7%) to drinking more than 60 g of ethanol a day, 291,800 (39.4%) to 20–60 g and 103,100 (13.9%; interval 82,600–207,200) to less than 20 g a day (up to about two drinks), including 41,300 (35,400–145,800) to drinking up to 10 g a day, of which 24,600 were in women, 14.3% of women's alcohol-attributed cancers. These are model estimates, not counts of people whose cancer was traced to drinking: they combine drinking estimated from 2010 per-capita consumption (recorded, unrecorded and tourist) and surveys, assumed to act 10 years later, with relative-risk curves for current drinking from World Cancer Research Fund reviews of observational studies, whose reference group the paper does not state, applied in the same way to every country; former drinkers carry no extra risk in the main analysis; the uncertainty intervals carry only the uncertainty in drinking and in the relative risks, leave out that in cancer incidence, the 10-year delay and the model's structure, and are lopsided for the low-intake figures; the hepatocellular share behind the liver figure comes from unpublished estimates; and the totals count harms only, a probable protective association with kidney cancer at intakes up to 30 g a day having been deliberately left out. Adding stomach and pancreatic cancer raised the total to 808,700, and counting former drinking raised it to 925,900, though the increment the paper gives for this (135,000) does not match its own totals. Earlier global estimates cited by the paper, for other years and with other choices, were 5.5% of new cancers in 2012 and 4.8% to 4.9% of cancer deaths in 2016 and 2019; an earlier model by an overlapping team, counting deaths from cancers of the mouth and oropharynx, oesophagus, colon and rectum, liver and breast and from other neoplasms, without the 2020 model's restriction to squamous cell and hepatocellular cancers, estimated 487 thousand cancer deaths caused by alcohol in 2004 (377 thousand in men, 111 thousand in women; no uncertainty intervals; Rehm et al., 2009); and in the Global Burden of Disease 2016 study, cancers made up 27.1% of the deaths attributed to alcohol in women aged 50 and older and 18.9% in men (Griswold et al., 2018). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.

set.statement: In adults in cohort studies and Italian case–control studies, mostly from the USA and Europe, drinking more alcohol on average is associated with a higher risk of liver cirrhosis that grows with the amount, compared with not drinking (lifetime or long-term abstainers) in two meta-analyses by one team, and compared with drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week in a Danish cohort whose women are also among the newer review's studies. None reports absolute risks by amount; in the Danish cohort (55,917 people aged 50 to 64 at the start, followed for a median of 14.9 years), 257 of 26,696 men (about 1 in 100) and 85 of 29,221 women (about 3 in 1,000) were diagnosed with alcoholic cirrhosis, 66 and 19 per 100,000 person-years, across all levels of drinking (Askgaard et al., 2015; editors' conversion). In the newer meta-analysis (Roerecke et al., 2019: seven cohorts, whose outcome was mostly death from cirrhosis, and two case–control studies; 2,629,272 people, 5,505 cases; one drink = 12 g of ethanol a day; funded by a US government institute), relative risks against long-term abstainers were 1.11 (95% CI 0.77–1.59) for occasional drinking, 1.40 (1.00–1.97) for one drink a day, 3.02 (1.95–4.70) for two, 3.27 (0.90–11.87) for three to four, 6.26 (2.38–16.50) for five to six and 10.70 (2.95–38.78) for seven or more, with I² from 70.6% to 98.6%, each category pooling four to six cohorts with 203 to 1,111 cases (editors' count from the forest plot; four cohorts and 276 cases at seven or more drinks); at seven or more drinks a day the three cohorts of men gave 1.80 (Chinese men) and 8.30 and 22.39 (two American cohorts), and in the two case–control studies 1 to 4 drinks a day gave 1.19 (0.58–2.43) and 9 to 13 drinks 7.36 (1.91–28.34). In the earlier meta-analysis (Rehm et al., 2010: 17 studies published 1980 to 2003, 3384 cases; against lifetime abstainers of the same sex), drinking more than 60 g a day (more than five drinks) went with relative risks of 22.7 (17.2–30.1) in women and 14 (11.7–16.7) in men in studies of cirrhosis death, and 6.1 (4.6–8.0) and 5.0 (3.9–6.4) in studies of diagnosed cirrhosis, of which there were at most six, four of them Italian (editors' count); in the Danish cohort, 28 to 42 drinks a week against fewer than 14 went with hazard ratios of 6.98 (4.65–10.5) in men and 16.2 (9.16–28.7) in women, adjusted for smoking, education and waist size. At up to about two drinks a day the sources disagree: in the earlier meta-analysis risk was raised in women's studies of cirrhosis death (1.9, 1.1–3.1, at up to 12 g a day; 5.6, 4.5–6.9, at 12 to 24 g), not raised in men's studies of cirrhosis death at up to 12 g a day (1.0, 0.6–1.6) but raised at 12 to 24 g (1.6, 1.4–2.0), not raised in women's studies of diagnosed cirrhosis (1.0, 0.5–1.9, at 12 to 24 g) and lower than in abstainers in men's studies of diagnosed cirrhosis (0.3, 0.2–0.4, at 12 to 24 g), which the authors could not explain biologically; the newer review's results found no clear sign of a threshold, with few studies to test one, though its discussion reports some evidence of one in men. The two meta-analyses share six studies (editors' comparison), intake was measured once, at the start, reference groups that included former drinkers were corrected upward (by an amount the earlier review does not report, and by about 1.24 in four cohorts of the newer review, editors' calculation), and the Danish cohort paper counted only cirrhosis recorded as alcoholic, whereas the newer review took that cohort's women with unspecified cirrhosis added (it lists 393 men and 229 women with either diagnosis, against 257 and 85 with alcoholic cirrhosis in the cohort paper). Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: The more people drank, the higher their risk of liver cirrhosis in these studies, compared with people who did not drink. In a Danish study of people aged 50 to 64, about 1 in 100 men and 3 in 1,000 women were diagnosed with alcohol-related cirrhosis over about 15 years. In a review of 9 studies, mostly counting deaths from cirrhosis, the risk was about 1.4 times as high at one drink a day (a drink being 12 g of alcohol; a borderline result), 3 times at two drinks and 11 times at seven or more drinks (a figure from 4 studies). How big the risk was differed a lot between studies: at seven or more drinks a day, from about 2 times to 22 times among men. At up to about two drinks a day, the studies disagree. Drinking was asked about only once, at the start.

set.population: Adults in cohort studies (among them American Cancer Society volunteers, health-plan members, nurses and physicians; baseline 1959 to 2005; outcome mostly cirrhosis death) and Italian hospital case–control studies, from the USA, Europe and Asia, in two meta-analyses of 17 and 9 studies by one team; and Danish-born adults aged 50 to 64 at the start (1993 to 1997) in the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort, whose women are also in the newer review
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Both meta-analyses are critically low on AMSTAR 2 (cards sc_rehm_2010, sc_roerecke_2019): no protocol; Rehm et al. did not appraise their studies; Roerecke et al. rated all but one cohort at moderate risk of bias (single baseline measure, observational design) and one, which dominates the women's high-intake estimates, at serious risk (adjusted for age only); viral hepatitis was taken into account in only one study of the newer review; part of each reference group is modelled by an upward correction for former drinkers; the Danish cohort (card sc_askgaard_2015, ROBINS-E high overall, its amount gradient being the most robust result) counts only cirrhosis recorded as alcoholic, which depends on known drinking (the newer review used the same cohort's wider outcome of alcoholic or unspecified cirrhosis, women only). Counted once.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; it is rated down one level each for risk of bias and inconsistency and up one level each for a large effect and a dose–response gradient, which gives low; a strict reading without the upgrades would give very low. Rated as worded: an association that grows with the amount, large at high intake; the claim does not say at what amount the risk begins, because the low-intake estimates conflict. Overlap: the two meta-analyses are by one team and share six studies, and the Danish cohort is one of the newer review's seven cohorts (its women only, with a wider outcome), so they are not three independent confirmations. Status replicated: the independent cohorts shown one by one in the newer review all point the same way at higher intake.

set.statement: In adults in the same cohorts and case–control studies, women who drank compared with women who did not had larger relative risks of liver cirrhosis than men who drank the same average amount compared with men who did not, in two meta-analyses by one team and a Danish cohort, but no source tested whether the difference between the sexes is larger than chance. In the earlier meta-analysis (against lifetime abstainers of the same sex; one drink = 12 g of ethanol), at 48 to 60 g a day (about five drinks) the relative risk was 14.7 (95% CI 11.0–19.6) in women and 7.0 (5.8–8.5) in men in studies of cirrhosis death, and 5.9 (3.7–9.3) and 2.3 (1.7–3.2) in studies of diagnosed cirrhosis (Rehm et al., 2010); in the newer one (against long-term abstainers of the same sex), 1.64 (1.07–2.51) in women and 0.91 (0.31–2.64) in men at one drink a day, 4.33 (2.59–7.25) and 1.97 (0.89–4.37) at two, and 24.58 (14.77–40.90) and 6.93 (1.07–44.99) at seven or more (Roerecke et al., 2019); and in the Danish cohort (against people of the same sex drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week), 3.49 (2.00–6.12) in women and 2.33 (1.52–3.58) in men at 14 to 28 drinks a week, and 16.2 (9.16–28.7) and 6.98 (4.65–10.5) at 28 to 42 (Askgaard et al., 2015). In the earlier meta-analysis the women's and men's intervals did not overlap at 8 of its 12 levels, including every level of cirrhosis death above 12 g a day (editors' comparison), but in the newer review and the Danish cohort they overlapped at every level; at two levels the men's figure was the higher (2.0 against 1.9 at 36 to 48 g a day in studies of diagnosed cirrhosis, and 1.23 against 0.95 for occasional drinking); in the newer review the women's estimates at five or more drinks a day rest mainly on one American cohort recruited in 1959–60 and adjusted only for age (52% and 77% of the weight), which is also the earlier review's largest study by number of people (548,185 women, 568 cases), though the newer review reports a similar rising pattern in the four women's cohorts adjusted for smoking and body size (figures in a supplement not read), and the men's estimates rest on two or three cohorts, which at one drink a day point in opposite directions; the earlier review counted three studies without results by sex for both sexes; and each relative risk is set against people of the same sex, so a larger ratio in women does not show that more women than men get cirrhosis at the same amount. No source gives absolute risks for women and men drinking the same amount; in the Danish cohort, alcoholic cirrhosis was diagnosed in 19 women and 66 men per 100,000 person-years, the women having drunk less (median 19 against 26 drinks a week among people who drank daily), and the authors say the 85 cases in women were too few for firm conclusions. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: In these studies, the same amount of drinking went with a bigger rise in cirrhosis risk for women than for men, each compared with people of their own sex who did not drink. For example, at about five drinks a day (48 to 60 g), studies of cirrhosis deaths found 14.7 times the risk for women and 7.0 times for men. In that older review the gap between women and men was bigger than the margins of error at most amounts; in a newer review and a Danish study it was not. No study tested whether this difference was more than chance, and much of the evidence on women who drank heavily came from one American study that began in 1959–60. A larger ratio does not mean that more women than men get cirrhosis: in a Danish study, fewer women than men were diagnosed (19 against 66 in 100,000 a year), and the women drank less. No study gave the risk, out of 100, for women and men who drink the same amount.

Roerecke et al. 2019, against long-term abstainers, women against men: occasional 0.95 (0.77–1.16) against 1.23 (0.46–3.28); 1 drink 1.64 (1.07–2.51) against 0.91 (0.31–2.64); 2 drinks 4.33 (2.59–7.25) against 1.97 (0.89–4.37); 3–4 drinks 3.87 (0.80–18.83) against 2.62 (0.42–16.21); 5–6 drinks 12.44 (6.65–23.27) against 3.80 (0.85–17.02); 7 or more 24.58 (14.77–40.90) against 6.93 (1.07–44.99). Askgaard et al. 2015, against fewer than 14 drinks a week of the same sex: 14–28 drinks a week 3.49 (2.00–6.12) against 2.33 (1.52–3.58); 28–42 drinks 16.2 (9.16–28.7) against 6.98 (4.65–10.5); incidence 19 against 66 per 100,000 person-years. Intervals: no overlap at 8 of the 12 levels in Rehm et al. (editors' comparison), overlap at every level in Roerecke et al. and Askgaard et al. No test of a sex difference in any source.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: No source tests whether the dose–response differs by sex; in Rehm et al. the women's and men's estimates come from partly different studies and three studies without results by sex were entered for both (card sc_rehm_2010); in Roerecke et al. the women's estimates at five or more drinks a day rest mainly on one 1959–60 cohort adjusted only for age, rated at serious risk of bias (card sc_roerecke_2019), which is also the largest study in Rehm et al.; each relative risk is set against the same sex's reference group, whose make-up and intake may differ between the sexes; women may under-report drinking more than men (a possibility the Danish authors raise, citing other studies).
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: In the newer review and the Danish cohort the women's and men's intervals overlap at every level (men 6.93, 1.07–44.99, at seven or more drinks a day; 85 cases in Danish women); only the earlier review gives intervals that do not overlap (8 of 12 levels, editors' comparison), and there the two sexes' estimates draw on partly different studies; no source tested the difference.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is rated down one level each for risk of bias and imprecision, which is below the floor, so very low. Rated as worded: higher relative risks in women than in men at the same average intake, a difference no source tested; the clearest separation, in the earlier review, comes from estimates that draw on partly different studies for each sex. Overlap: the Danish cohort is inside the newer review, and the two reviews share six studies, among them the 1959–60 American cohort of women that carries most of the newer review's weight at high intake; but the earlier review's studies and the Danish cohort are independent of each other and agree in direction, hence status replicated.

set.statement: In middle-aged Danish adults followed for about 15 years (55,917 people aged 50 to 64 at the start, 1993 to 1997; 35% of those invited took part), drinking every day compared with drinking on two to four days a week, with the weekly amount (in 12-g drinks), smoking, education and waist size taken into account, is associated with a higher risk of a register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis in men, but not clearly in women, in one cohort study (Askgaard et al., 2015; no funding stated, no conflicts declared). In men, 171 of 7276 who drank daily and 27 of 9165 who drank on two to four days a week were diagnosed (about 2 in 100 against 3 in 1,000; editors' calculation), but those who drank daily also drank more (median 26 against 8.9 drinks a week): the hazard ratio for daily drinking was 8.29 (95% CI 5.52–12.4) adjusted for age, 4.83 (3.20–7.29) with amount added and 3.65 (2.39–5.55) with smoking, education and waist size as well, while drinking on five or six days a week did not differ clearly from two to four (1.43, 0.84–2.43). In women, 30 of 3931 who drank daily and 15 of 9481 who drank on two to four days a week were diagnosed (about 8 in 1,000 against 2 in 1,000; editors' calculation); with amount and the other factors taken into account, daily drinking gave 1.73 (0.85–3.52) and drinking on five or six days 2.30 (1.14–4.67), with no trend across frequencies (P = 0.14), and the extra risk per weekly drink was largest in women who drank least often (1.09 per drink, against 1.05 in women who drank daily). How often and how much people drank were closely linked (correlation 0.77 in men and 0.85 in women), people who drank daily drank somewhat more even within the same amount category, and the authors say this makes the two hard to separate; in the main analysis amount entered the model as a single continuous term although risk rose steeply with amount, so some confounding by amount may remain (editors' reading); drinking was asked about once, at the start, and binge drinking could not be studied. A 2019 review reports, for this cohort, daily drinking against two to four days a week at the same weekly amount as 2.25 (1.68–3.00) in men and 1.28 (0.82–2.02) in women, figures that are not in the cohort paper's main text; the review lists the cohort with 393 cases in men and 229 in women, the counts of the cohort paper's supplementary analysis of alcoholic or unspecified cirrhosis, so its figures probably come from that analysis (editors' reading; the supplement is not on file). For a large British cohort of women who drank (the Million Women Study, not read here), the review reports 1.61 (1.40–1.85) for daily against non-daily drinking and 0.69 (0.62–0.77) for drinking with meals against outside meals, associations it calls similar across groups by body size, smoking and beverage without saying what they were adjusted for, and 2.47 (1.96–3.11) for drinking both daily and outside meals, adjusted for amount and beverage type (Roerecke et al., 2019). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.

set.statement: In the world's population, alcohol use compared with no alcohol use is estimated by two global models to account for about 2.3 million (2004, after subtracting deaths the model counted as prevented; editors' rounding) to 2.8 million (2016) deaths a year. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016 (95% uncertainty interval 2.4–3.3 million), 2.2% of age-standardised deaths in women and 6.8% in men, about 2 and 7 in every 100; it ranked alcohol seventh among risk factors overall and first at ages 15 to 49, where 3.8% of women's and 12.2% of men's deaths were attributed to it, the leading causes being tuberculosis, road injuries and self-harm (Griswold et al., 2018; funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, with support from the US National Institute on Aging). A comparative risk assessment for 2004, which applied the attributable fractions of WHO's assessments for 2000 and 2002 to WHO's 2004 death estimates, estimated 2482 thousand deaths caused by alcohol, less 227 thousand deaths it modelled as prevented (215 thousand from heart and blood-vessel disease, 12 thousand from diabetes), leaving 2255 thousand, 3.8 in every 100 deaths worldwide (6.3 in 100 deaths of men and 1.1 in 100 of women) and 5.3 in 100 deaths before the age of 60; the deaths caused were mainly from unintentional injuries (666 thousand), heart and blood-vessel disease (545 thousand), cancer (487 thousand), liver cirrhosis (373 thousand) and intentional injuries (272 thousand) (Rehm et al., 2009; supported by the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto, the underlying assessments by WHO and the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health; no conflicts declared). These are model estimates, not counted deaths: they combine estimated drinking (sales data, estimates of unrecorded alcohol, which is more than a quarter of the world's drinking, and surveys) with relative-risk curves from observational studies (for the 2004 model, mostly of middle-class cohorts in high-income countries), applied to every population. The 2004 estimate has no uncertainty intervals, although its authors describe the uncertainty as fairly low, citing an earlier WHO report, and the 2016 intervals carry sampling error and the uncertainty of the model's parameters but are not said to include uncertainty from the model's structure or from bias in the underlying studies; the same group's next round, cited from unpublished work in a 2022 paper, put deaths in 2020 at 1.78 million (1.39–2.27 million), below the 2016 interval (Bryazka et al., 2022; not read in its own source); the net figures depend on protective heart and diabetes estimates at low intake, which the 2004 authors call controversial; the 2016 figure is counted against a minimum-risk level of zero drinks a day, whose interval reached 0.8 drinks (10 g each) a day and which moved to about half a drink a day when the same group updated its weights (0.534, 0–1.00; Bryazka et al., 2022); the 2016 authors expect their figures to be underestimates, because unrecorded drinking may still be missed, drinking patterns were not modelled, and harm to others from violence, people under 15 and some outcomes, such as dementia, were left out; and the estimates used different methods and inputs, so the differences between them are not a trend. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
set.plain: Two global models estimated that alcohol caused about 2.3 to 2.8 million deaths a year, compared with no one drinking. The Global Burden of Disease study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016: about 7 in 100 deaths of men and 2 in 100 of women. At ages 15 to 49, alcohol was the top risk factor in that study (about 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women), the leading causes being tuberculosis, road injuries and self-harm. An older model using WHO data estimated about 2.5 million deaths caused in 2004, minus about 0.2 million it counted as prevented, mainly from heart disease; that is about 4 in 100 of all deaths. Injuries, heart and blood-vessel disease, cancer and liver cirrhosis made up most of the deaths caused. A later round of the Global Burden of Disease study, quoted second-hand, put the figure at about 1.8 million deaths in 2020. These are computer estimates, not counted deaths. They rely on studies of groups of people (for the older model, mostly in richer countries), and the models used different methods, so the numbers cannot be compared as a trend.
set.magnitude: Griswold et al. 2018 (GBD 2016; 95% uncertainty intervals): 2.8 million (2.4–3.3) deaths in 2016; 2.2% (1.5–3.0) of age-standardised female and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; 1.6% (1.4–2.0) and 6.0% (5.4–6.7) of DALYs; ages 15–49: 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths; leading attributable causes at 15–49: tuberculosis 1.4% (1.0–1.7), road injuries 1.2% (0.7–1.9) and self-harm 1.1% (0.6–1.5) of total deaths; minimum-risk level 0 (0.0–0.8) standard drinks of 10 g a day. Rehm et al. 2009 (WHO comparative risk assessment, 2004; thousands; no intervals): caused 2482 (men 2039, women 443); prevented 227 (cardiovascular 215, diabetes 12); net 2255 (men 1944, women 311) of 58 738 deaths, 3.8% (men 6.3%, women 1.1%); under age 60, 5.3% (men 7.9%, women 1.9%); deaths caused by cause: unintentional injuries 666, cardiovascular 545, cancer 487, cirrhosis 373, intentional injuries 272, neuropsychiatric 135, perinatal 3. Bryazka et al. 2022: global minimum-risk level 0.534 (0–1.00) drinks a day with the GBD 2016 curves and GBD 2020 weights; citing unpublished GBD 2020 work, 1.78 million (1.39–2.27) deaths in 2020.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: The two models give figures of similar size (2.3 to 2.8 million a year) for different years and with different methods. The second-hand 2020 figure from the same GBD group (1.78 million) is lower; it reflects changed curves and weights as much as time, and is covered under imprecision.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: No uncertainty intervals in the 2004 model; the 2016 intervals (2.4 to 3.3 million) are not said to include structural uncertainty or bias in the underlying studies. The next round of the same model, cited second-hand, gives 1.78 million (1.39–2.27) for 2020, below the 2016 interval, which shows how much the figure moves with the model's choices.
set.grade.reasoning: Model estimates are not graded as evidence of an effect: the claim describes what the models estimate (relation describes), and its certainty comes from the observational evidence behind the relative-risk curves (low), rated down for the models' indirectness and their incomplete uncertainty, which gives very low. No upgrade applies to a modelled count. Status replicated by the same team, under the flag's shared analysis model (METHODS §6.4) rather than shared investigators: the 2016 and 2004 estimates come from different groups, but both use the comparative-risk-assessment method, the 2016 exposure model follows the approach of Rehm and colleagues (Griswold et al., Methods › Data sources, 2nd paragraph), and both draw on much the same cohort literature and WHO consumption data, so their agreement is not independent replication (METHODS §6.3); the second-hand 2020 figure comes from the GBD group itself and is not counted.
